extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, patent illustrators, and IP professionals seeking guidance on CAD/patent drawings
extracted.subtask_short: creating patent CAD and drawing files
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing patent drawings and CAD/3‑D files suitable for patent applications and downstream product development, including software selection, view types, file formats, and prototyping considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are an essential element of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are not only the beginning of everything in patent. They also facilitate the attorney creativity process by describing what the product is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure drawings clearly describe the invention's functional characteristics; poor or insufficient drawings may initiate iterations and increase chances of PTO rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure output drawings contain sufficient detail
rubrics_metrics.description: If output drawing is not having enough details in your output, it may initiate iterations and consequently there are chances of getting a rejection from PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust and save drawing media characteristics (line thickness, line type, etc.) using software to achieve required detail level; include overall dimensions to judge product shape and aspect ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose software appropriate to the task
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate software based on requirements like CorelDraw, AutoCAD, Adobe Illustrator, OmniGraffle and Visio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick tools according to need: vector illustration, 3‑D modelling, diagramming, or raster editing. Consider compatibility with the required output format (vector vs raster) and downstream uses (manufacturing, prototyping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 3‑D models / CAD for manufacturing and prototyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Without 3‑D model, it’s difficult to get to the manufacturing stage. The purpose of 3‑D model is not only to be able to see what your idea would look like but to be able to provide you a manufacturer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have 3‑D models, extract required views from CAD models; 3‑D models enable rapid prototyping, accurate representations, and facilitate manufacturers and product development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide all dimensional detail needed for production
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet the input requirements for design and development depict the same invention. You need all dimensional detail for mapping the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design outputs (drawings/specifications/manufacturing instructions) should describe components, assemblies, sub-assemblies, and product acceptance criteria; include specific characteristics essential for safe and proper use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer vector images for scalability and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Vector images are digital artwork where points, lines and curves scale without loss of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vector formats (PDF, EPS, SVG, AI) for drawings to avoid resolution loss when resizing; raster images (JPEG, PNG, TIFF, PSD) will distort if enlarged. Choose vector tools (Illustrator, CorelDraw) when scalable crisp graphics are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select raster vs vector based on source and end-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the output format and based on that decide which software to use; it will be a raster image or a vector image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For photo-like images or pixel editing use raster editors (Photoshop); for line art, schematics, and patent drawings use vector editors. Converting raster to vector may lose information—choose original appropriate format when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AutoCAD for accurate 2‑D/3‑D models and extracting multi‑views
rubrics_metrics.description: AutoCAD is highly customizable and supports many CAD formats; you can go back and forth from 2‑D to 3‑D and extract planar views from 3‑D models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AutoCAD to produce accurate representations, proper shading, textures, and to extract standard views (plan, front, side, back, bottom) for manufacturing and prototyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include standard multi‑view projections (plan/front/side)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common way to communicate information is by using three different views in a multi view drawing: front view, top view and side views. Other views are back and bottom views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce mutually perpendicular planar projections; include overall dimensions and aspect ratios so the product shape is unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sectional views when internal details are needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Sectional view is used on drawings to show an area of hidden parts of an object by cutting away or removing some partial objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parts are assembled and hidden lines become confusing, add sectional views; include the cutting edge and an arrow to show where the sectional view is taken from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exploded views to show components and assembly order
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploded view shows the components of an object, relations and order of assembly; parts are separated by little distance with imaginary lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select perspective angles to cover major parts and features and use imaginary lines to indicate assembly relationships and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create duplicate/unornamented views when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate of the view is created without the annotation and detailing items; plane and unornamented views are simple and undecorated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clean duplicates for clarity or for use in different contexts (e.g., one with annotations and one without).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include flat object views for planar parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat object views allow the user to fill out the details and save the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For planar or thin objects provide flat views showing detail and dimensions appropriate for manufacturing or inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate shading and rendering to show texture/material
rubrics_metrics.description: We know how to use exact shading techniques that can identify and illustrate textures as well as surface material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply shading carefully to increase image sharpness and to communicate surface characteristics useful for understanding function or manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep patent drawings focused; limit industrial design detail but include some for development
rubrics_metrics.description: We're not adding industrial design details in your patent drawings but it should have 15 to 25% for the process of product development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent drawings should not become full industrial design drawings but may include modest design detail (approx. 15–25%) to aid product development without compromising patent focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CorelDraw features for object-level editing and vector work
rubrics_metrics.description: CorelDraw is a vector graphic editor where each object can be edited separately; it includes bitmap-image editor and wide editing tools to adjust colour and contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CorelDraw when you need per-object edits, selective enhancements, or hybrid vector/bitmap workflows; choose versions with the needed file compatibility (.cdr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage Adobe Illustrator for in-panel editing, artboards, and scalability
rubrics_metrics.description: Adobe Illustrator allows in-panel editing, multiple artboards, creates scalable vector graphics without resolution issues, and has 3‑D functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Illustrator for professional vector graphics, logos, and multi-image compositions; be aware that converting raster to vector may lose information and that Illustrator has limited native raster support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Microsoft Visio for diagrams, consistency, and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Visio helps draw diagrams faster, maintains consistency with Office apps, provides diagram templates and can spot common errors using diagram validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Visio for flowcharts, workflows, and data‑connected diagrams; use validation and rule sets (e.g., start/terminate shapes for SharePoint workflows) to enforce standards and to catch common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare virtual prototypes and use 3‑D printing for iteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a virtual prototype is the first process of iteration through the design, followed by physical prototypes; 3‑D printing converts designs to samples with lower cost and quick turnaround.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use digital models to iterate quickly and test manufacturability; coordinate software, hardware, and materials to move from CAD to physical prototypes and to get pricing/quotes for production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure file format compatibility for downstream processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Most files fit into raster or vector categories; choose formats that downstream tools and manufacturers accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm accepted file types before sending (AI, PDF, STEP/IGES for CAD, raster formats for photos); provide formats that preserve dimensions and geometry needed for manufacturing and prototyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust and save drawing characteristics (line thickness, type)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can adjust and save the characteristic of your drawing media such as line thickness, line type, etc., by using software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize and save style settings so drawings are consistent and meet any formal drawing requirements; use software presets or templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perspective views appropriately (one/two/three‑point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspective is a technique for depicting three-dimensional volumes on two dimensions; there are typically one, two, and three point perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the right perspective (two‑point commonly used) to communicate the object’s spatial relationships; use perspective for illustrative purposes, not for precise manufacturing dimensions.
